interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through everything that happens between typing a URL and the page appearing.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
⭐ **Q: Walk me through everything that happens between typing a URL and the page appearing?**

I'd structure it as six phases in order, naming what each one does and why it has to happen before the next: DNS resolves the hostname to an IP; the packet routes hop-by-hop to that IP; TCP does a three-way handshake to open a reliable connection; TLS layers an encrypted channel on top of that connection; the browser sends the HTTP request and gets a response; the browser then parses and renders it.

I'd also flag the caveat that this full chain rarely runs end-to-end — a CDN edge might serve the response without ever reaching the origin, and a warm connection skips the TCP/TLS handshakes entirely on a second request to the same host.

**Testing:** whether you can chain multiple networking concepts into one coherent narrative, not just recite each piece in isolation.

interviewQuestions.question: Why does the second page load on a site usually feel faster than the first?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
**Q: Why does the second page load on a site usually feel faster than the first?**

I'd point to connection reuse: the first request pays for DNS resolution, a TCP handshake, and a TLS handshake — each an extra round-trip before any data moves. If the connection stays open (HTTP keep-alive), the second request to the same host skips all three and goes straight to the HTTP exchange.

Concretely, on a 150ms-latency mobile connection, that's roughly 450-600ms saved on the second request alone — often more than the actual page content takes to transfer. This is exactly why browsers keep connections alive and why HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple requests over one connection instead of opening a new one per resource.

**Testing:** whether you understand connection setup cost as a real, quantifiable overhead — not an abstract detail.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why warm connections are faster
